overview: The Abipones were peoples of the Chaco, especially its southern frontier, organised through local groups and shifting alliances rather than one central kingdom. Their history combines hunting, gathering, skilled making and extensive exchange. Horses, iron tools, colonial missions and provincial governments changed that world without producing one universal date of conquest.

periods.title: Negotiating life around missions
periods.summary: From the middle eighteenth century, Abipón groups entered settlements known as reducciones. These could provide food, exchange and protection, while residents continued to pursue interests that differed from the missionaries’ plans.

periods.title: After Jesuit administration
periods.summary: The Jesuits left Concepción in 1767. Other clergy maintained the settlement into the nineteenth century, when it also became a frontier fort. Changes in administration varied between settlements.

periods.title: Violence and regrouping
periods.summary: An attack devastated San Jerónimo del Rey in 1818. Abipón groups nevertheless regrouped and continued negotiating with provincial governments; this settlement’s destruction was not the end of the people.

periods.title: Agreements at El Sauce
periods.summary: Agreements with Santa Fe’s governor Estanislao López in 1824 led groups toward settlement at San Jerónimo del Sauce. Their relationship with provincial authority remained negotiated and unstable.

periods.title: Resistance and dispersal
periods.summary: In 1836, some residents left El Sauce. Subsequent rebellion, dispersal and returns reveal the limits of provincial control and divisions within Abipón society.

items.text: Hunting, fishing and gathering supported households, with fruit, roots and honey alongside meat. Lucaioli cautions that surviving documents cannot establish the exact balance of these foods before European contact. Later increases in cattle and the use of horses changed available choices.

One account describes families drying animals’ skins near a lake while collecting honey in nearby woods. Lucaioli uses this example to show that expeditions could combine several tasks and include whole families, complicating a simple picture of men hunting alone.

sections.title: Making containers, clothing and useful tools

items.text: Dobrizhoffer described Abipón women shaping clay pots and pitchers by hand. Vitar examines this testimony as evidence of skilled work that colonial writers often undervalued. It is a written description of production, not an identification of a particular excavated vessel.

Women prepared skins for clothing and worked wool into dyed textiles. The equipment described for Abipón weaving included portable cane and wooden pieces that could be carried on horseback. Mobility therefore did not prevent technically demanding manufacture.

Mission authorities used existing textile skills to demand regular labour and to supply clothing. Vitar shows how colonial praise for women’s industry also served attempts to control their time. The adoption of wool and cotton did not mean that missionaries had invented weaving for them.

Horses enabled longer journeys and the transport of more goods. Cattle and horses also became exchange goods for salt, tools, weapons, clothing and yerba. Lucaioli and Nesis describe these connections as growing economic interdependence between Indigenous groups and colonial society.

The researchers distinguish community cattle used for food, herds held by influential leaders and animals acquired for trade. These categories matter because a mission’s herd was not simply a measure of every resident’s personal wealth. Different animals supported different social obligations.

Concepción’s buildings included a chapel and missionaries’ rooms, but also carpentry and blacksmithing workshops and mills. The local museum’s account makes clear that the settlement involved practical production as well as religious instruction.

The same account records repeated relocation of Concepción in response to environmental difficulties and conflict. Its changing sites illustrate why a mission’s name should not be treated as one permanently occupied town with fixed borders.

Letters and inventories can expose the practical arrangements behind a mission. A 1748 San Jerónimo founding record listed cattle, sheep, carts, oxen, axes and a portable altar, placing food, transport and tools alongside worship in plans for the settlement.

Green’s study uses correspondence, military reports and financial records to reassess the 1836 to 1838 conflict. He finds that settlement at El Sauce did not imply unconditional submission: groups retained distinct leaders and could leave, negotiate or resist.

ending.text: Missions, warfare, displacement and incorporation into provincial society transformed Abipón communities unevenly. The nineteenth-century record shows both resistance and assimilation, rather than a single surrender by a unified state. Destruction of one settlement cannot establish that every Abipón person or descendant disappeared.

sources.title: Carina Paula Lucaioli, Los grupos abipones hacia mediados del siglo XVIII, 2005
sources.note: Chapters on territory and economic strategies, printed pages 91 to 140. A critical reading of colonial accounts, not direct access to an unchanged precolonial society.

sources.title: Beatriz Vitar, Hilar, teñir y tejer, 2015
sources.note: Anuario de Estudios Americanos 72(2), especially pages 672 to 675 and 683 to 686. Abipón examples are distinguished from neighbouring peoples discussed in the same article.

sources.note: Andes 18; sections on mission formation and types of cattle ownership. Abipón and Mocoví economies are compared rather than collapsed into one people.

sources.title: Centro Cultural del Bicentenario, Sala de Abipones
sources.note: Local museum account of Concepción’s relocations, workshops and change of administration. Livestock totals and an ambiguous sequence of moves are excluded.

sources.note: Revista TEFROS 19(1), pages 88 to 111, especially 93 and 108. Nineteenth-century political transformation is not equated with biological extinction.
